title: How Junk Mail Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with the Austin, Texas "Free Paper" junk mail art installation by Anet Lawrence at Flatbed Press Art Gallery, and Barbara Hashimoto's Chicago "Junk Mail with Grand Piano" piece. They then cover junk mail's harms: identity theft from pre-approved credit card offers, the waste of paper and the energy and water used to make it (including the claim that about 250,000 homes could be heated by burning a day's junk mail), and the paper-making water process. They discuss the pharmaceutical direct mail market, how to return junk mail marked address correction requested or return postage guaranteed, the Opt Out Prescreen site, the Direct Marketing Association's consumer opt-out site, how personal lists are sold by credit bureaus, warranty cards and sucker lists, and the paid service Green Dimes. The episode closes with a pointer to an MSNBC article by Sig Kerscheimer and a How Stuff Works article on stopping junk mail.

segments.title: Junk mail art installations
segments.summary: Opening banter. The hosts describe Anet Lawrence's Free Paper installation in Austin, Texas, made from a year of junk mail, and Barbara Hashimoto's Chicago piece in which a pianist plays while shredded junk mail is dumped on his piano.

segments.title: Harms of junk mail: identity theft and energy
segments.summary: The hosts say junk mail is annoying and harmful. They cite identity theft tied to pre-approved credit card offers, a figure attributed to consumer advocate Sig Kerscheimer, and how they dispose of mail (shredding, burning). They note a claim that burning a day's junk mail could heat 250,000 homes.

segments.title: Paper waste and water use in papermaking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss paper waste, including a claim about a wall twelve feet tall stretching from New York to Los Angeles made from annual paper waste, and the large amount of water used in papermaking, around 28 billion gallons a year, with a 200-to-1 water-to-pulp ratio. They note about a hundred million trees a year are used for paper, citing the University of Oregon, and that mills reuse water.

segments.title: Direct mail pharmaceutical marketing
segments.summary: The hosts mention that direct mail advertising for pharmaceuticals was a roughly ten billion dollar market in 2008, with a return of about ten dollars and twenty-seven cents per dollar spent.

segments.title: Returning junk mail and opt-out options
segments.summary: The hosts explain that bulk mail stamped address correction requested or return postage guaranteed can be returned unopened by writing refused and returning it to the mailbox. Solicitations with reply envelopes can be sent back asking for removal. They note there is no national do-not-mail registry.

segments.title: Opt-out services and how personal lists are sold
segments.summary: The hosts explain that name and address lists are valuable when aggregated, and credit reporting bureaus can share certain information. They recommend Opt Out Prescreen, which stops the four major credit bureaus from selling data, and the Direct Marketing Association's consumer opt-out site.

segments.title: Warranty cards, sucker lists, and Greendimes
segments.summary: The hosts warn against filling out warranty cards and responding to sweepstakes mailings, which can put people on sucker lists. They describe Greendimes, a service charging about twenty dollars a year that handles removal requests and plants trees.

segments.title: Closing and further reading
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the MSNBC article by Sig Kerscheimer and a How Stuff Works article on stopping junk mail, then sign off.
